screens.title: What is an algorithm?
screens.narratorSegment: An algorithm is a clear, finite set of instructions that transforms input into output. The recipe analogy is useful: the ingredients are inputs, the ordered instructions are the algorithm, and the finished dish is the output. A correct algorithm must terminate and produce the intended result for all valid inputs. In practice, algorithms vary by style — some are iterative, some recursive — but what unites them is determinism and clarity: each step is defined so a computer can execute it. Understanding this definition matters because it separates the idea of correctness from other concerns like implementation details or performance. For example, two algorithms can both solve the same problem correctly, but one may use a loop and the other recursion; both are valid if they terminate and provide the right output for all inputs. A common misconception is to confuse a program or a line of code with an algorithm; think instead of the overall procedure. Finally, notice why explicit steps are important: they let us reason about resources like time and memory, which we analyze next. How would you describe the steps for finding an item on a shelf as an algorithmic recipe?

keyIdea.text: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that transforms inputs to outputs and terminates.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is an algorithm?
Definition
An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined instructions that takes input and produces output. It must terminate and be unambiguous so a machine can follow it.
Analogy: Recipe
Ingredients are inputs, steps are instructions, the dish is the output. The recipe must finish to be valid.
Why this matters
Precise steps allow reasoning about correctness and resource use, independent of programming language.
Common misconception
A single line of code is not an algorithm by itself; the algorithm is the whole step-by-step plan the code implements.
Key Takeaway

Algorithms are recipes: explicit, finite instructions that let us reason about correctness and performance.

Concrete example: Finding a book on a shelf
Steps: 1) Pick a starting shelf, 2) Scan each book title in order, 3) If title matches, stop and return location, 4) If end reached, report not found. This simple procedure is an algorithm because it is finite and unambiguous.
Check your understanding
  • Does the procedure always stop? If it scans a finite shelf, yes.
  • Are steps unambiguous? Each comparison is clearly defined.
  • Is it the same as optimized search? No — it's a straightforward sequential approach.
Reflect: Where might this algorithm be fine, and when might its performance be a problem?

screens.title: Efficiency: Time and Space
screens.narratorSegment: Efficiency in algorithms refers to two primary resources: time and space. Time is how many computational steps an algorithm requires, typically as a function of input size. Space is how much memory an algorithm needs while it runs. Both matter because a correct algorithm can still be unusable if it demands too much time or memory for realistic inputs. For example, an algorithm that looks fine on a list of ten items might become impractical when that list contains millions. When evaluating efficiency we focus on how requirements grow as input size grows — this reveals scaling behavior. A common beginner mistake is to consider only raw execution time on one machine or on small inputs. That can hide exponential or quadratic growth that quickly becomes impractical. When choosing between algorithms, consider trade-offs: sometimes a faster algorithm needs more memory, and sometimes conserving space costs time. Being able to reason about these trade-offs helps you select the right approach for the problem constraints you face. Ask yourself: what happens to run time and memory when input size doubles? Efficiency: Time and Space means time and space costs determine whether a correct algorithm scales to real inputs; analyze both when choosing solutions.. In practical terms, why we measure resource use and how it affects practical choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Efficiency: Time and Space
What to measure
Time: the number of elementary operations as input size grows. Space: additional memory used beyond inputs. Both are functions of the input size 'n'.
Practical example
Two sorting algorithms may both sort correctly, but one may need less time for large arrays. That difference decides which one you use in production.
Trade-offs
Sometimes faster algorithms use more memory. Choose based on your constraints: CPU time or available memory.
Common mistake
Testing only on small inputs can hide poor scaling. Always consider growth with larger 'n'.
Key Takeaway

Measure both time and space as functions of input size to predict real-world performance.

Scenario: Doubling input size
If an algorithm's time grows linearly, doubling the input roughly doubles the time. If it grows quadratically, doubling input multiplies time by four. This illustrates why growth behavior is more important than raw times on a single run.
Check your intuition
  • Would you pick an algorithm that takes hours for realistic input sizes even if it is simple? Usually no.
  • Could a small optimization change quadratic behavior to linear? Often yes, and that is a valuable goal.
Reflect: Which resource constraint is most important for the applications you use every day?

screens.title: Big O notation and common complexity classes
screens.narratorSegment: Big O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's growth rate as input size 'n' becomes large. It abstracts away constant factors and low-order terms so we focus on how runtime or space scales. O(1) means constant time: the operation's cost does not depend on n, such as reading a single array element by index. O(log n) is logarithmic and often appears when an algorithm repeatedly halves the problem, for example in binary search on sorted data. O(n) is linear: cost grows proportionally with the number of items, like scanning every element in a list. O(n log n) commonly shows up in efficient comparison-based sorting algorithms and combines linear and logarithmic behavior. O(n^2) is quadratic and appears in simple nested loops, where doubling n roughly quadruples the work. A key practical point is that, for large n, the highest-order term dominates: we say n^2 grows much faster than n. A common misconception is treating Big O as precise timing; it is a classification of growth, not a stopwatch. Think about which class an algorithm falls into when deciding whether it will scale to larger datasets.

keyIdea.text: Big O abstracts growth: constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, and quadratic are common classes to recognize for scaling decisions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Big O notation
Complexity cards
O(1) — Constant
Time does not depend on input size. Example: accessing an array element by index.
O(log n) — Logarithmic
Halving or reducing search space repeatedly. Example: binary search on sorted arrays.
O(n) — Linear
Proportional to input size. Example: scanning every element in a list.
More classes and intuition
O(n log n)
Combines linear work with logarithmic steps. Often appears in efficient sorts like mergesort and quicksort on average.
O(n^2) — Quadratic
Nested loops over the input. Example: simple comparison-based double loop over a list of n items.
Misconception
Big O is not exact runtime; it classifies growth and ignores constants and lower-order terms.
Key Takeaway

Recognize common growth patterns so you can predict how algorithms scale as input size increases.

screens.title: Best, Worst and Average Cases
screens.narratorSegment: When analyzing an algorithm, we consider three common cases: best, worst, and average. The best case describes inputs for which the algorithm does the least work. For example, a linear search finds the target at the first position — that is O(1) work. The worst case describes inputs that force the algorithm to do the most work; for linear search that is when the target is last or missing, which yields O(n) comparisons. The average case considers typical inputs assuming a probability distribution; for linear search with a uniformly random target present, you expect about n over 2 comparisons, which Big O simplifies to O(n). We usually report worst-case complexity because it provides a guarantee: no matter the input, the algorithm will not be slower than that bound. A common misconception is assuming average-case measurements guarantee performance in adversarial settings; they do not. Choosing to focus on worst-case is a conservative decision that helps when inputs may be adversarial or unpredictable. Reflect: can you think of an algorithm where average-case is more informative than worst-case? In practical terms, how to think about different inputs and why worst-case is often used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Best, Worst, Average
Step-by-step comparison
Best case
Minimal work scenario. Example: linear search finds the target at the first index — constant time.
Worst case
Maximal work scenario. Example: linear search examines all elements when the target is not present — linear time.
Average case
Expected work for typical inputs. For uniform random target positions in linear search, expect about n/2 comparisons.
Why report worst-case?
Worst-case complexity provides an upper bound and a guarantee. It is especially important when inputs might be adversarial or extreme. Average-case can be useful when inputs are known to follow a distribution, but it offers weaker guarantees.
Misconception check
Don't assume a good average-case means the algorithm is safe in all situations. If a rare worst-case is catastrophic for your application, you must account for it.
Key Takeaway

Best, worst, and average cases describe different input scenarios; worst-case gives a conservative performance guarantee.

screens.title: Linear search explained
screens.narratorSegment: Linear search is the most straightforward way to find a target in an unsorted list: check each element in sequence until you either find the target or reach the end. Start at the first element, compare it to the target, and if it matches return its index. If not, move to the next element and repeat. This method always terminates for a finite list. Its simplicity is its strength: it requires no preprocessing or sorted order. The trade-off is efficiency: in the worst case it examines every element, giving O(n) time complexity. A useful concrete example is searching for a name in an unsorted contact list; you scan entries one by one. A common misconception is that linear search is always slow; for small lists or when targets are frequently near the front it can be perfectly acceptable. When choosing linear search, ask whether the list is unsorted and whether occasional linear scans are acceptable for your expected input sizes. Linear search explained means checks elements sequentially until a match is found or the list ends. correct and simple, with worst-case o(n) time.. In practical terms, a simple algorithm that checks each element until it finds the target. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Linear search
Process steps
  1. Start at the first element of the list.
  2. Compare current element to the target.
  3. If equal, return the index and stop.
  4. If not, advance to the next element and repeat.
  5. If end reached without finding it, return a sentinel meaning not found.
Concrete scenario
Searching an unsorted list of phone numbers for a contact when you don't want to sort the list first.
Reflect: If your list were kept sorted and you had many searches, what change might you make?
Explanation and takeaway
Linear search requires no setup and always works on unsorted data. Its average and worst-case time complexity are linear in the number of elements, so it scales poorly for large lists. However, for small datasets or one-off searches it is simple and clear.
Common mistake
Assuming linear search is unacceptable in all cases. Consider dataset size and frequency of searches before replacing it with more complex solutions.
Key Takeaway

Linear search is simple and correct for unsorted lists but has linear worst-case time; choose it for small or infrequent searches.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Linear search in C
Code (C) — linear_search
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h> // For boolean type

// Function to perform linear search
int linear_search(int arr[], int size, int target) {
  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    if (arr[i] == target) {
      return i; // Target found at index i
    }
  }
  return -1; // Target not found
}

int main() {
  int numbers[] = {10, 5, 8, 12, 3, 7};
  int size = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
  int target1 = 8;
  int target2 = 99;

  int result1 = linear_search(numbers, size, target1);
  if (result1 != -1) {
    printf("Target %d found at index %d.
", target1, result1);
  } else {
    printf("Target %d not found.
", target1);
  }

fullNarratorScript:
Algorithms are step-by-step procedures that tell a computer how to solve a problem. Think of them as recipes: inputs are your ingredients, instructions are precise steps, and outputs are the finished dish. In this chapter you will learn to identify the defining characteristics of an algorithm, why we care about efficiency as inputs grow, and how Big O notation gives us a shared vocabulary to compare scaling behavior independent of hardware. You will see concrete examples of constant, linear, logarithmic, and quadratic growth, and we will trace a simple linear search both conceptually and in C code. Understanding these ideas helps you choose algorithms that remain practical as data grows, avoid common misconceptions like confusing best-case behavior with typical performance, and reason about trade-offs between time and memory. By the end of this lesson you will be able to express an algorithm's time complexity using Big O, explain best, worst and average cases, and analyze a linear search on arrays and arrays of strings. Consider which part of a program will slow down first as your data grows — that is usually where algorithmic thinking pays off.

This page lists measurable objectives that will guide your learning. First, you will be able to define what an algorithm is and recognize its key characteristics such as clear steps, inputs, and outputs. Being precise about what an algorithm is helps you describe program behavior and reason about correctness. Second, you will explain why efficiency matters: time and space costs determine whether a solution works on small examples only or scales to real data. This matters because the same correct algorithm can be unusable if it grows too quickly with input size. Third, you will learn Big O notation to describe the limiting growth of runtime or memory as input size increases. Big O lets you compare algorithms independently of hardware and small implementation details. Finally on this screen, you will begin to distinguish best, worst, and average cases for performance, which is essential for setting expectations about runtime in typical and adversarial scenarios. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a milestone you can use to verify your competency.

Continuing the objectives, you will analyze the efficiency of a linear search using Big O notation. That means you will determine best, worst, and average case runtimes for linear search and explain why we typically report worst-case complexity when comparing algorithms. You will also adapt and implement linear search for strings and consider how string comparison cost affects overall complexity. For example, comparing very long strings can add extra cost proportional to their length, and you should account for that in your time analysis. Lastly, you will practice reasoning about scaling through a short hands-on activity: modify the provided C starter to search arrays of strings and justify the complexity of your implementation. These skills combine conceptual understanding with a concrete coding practice so you can both reason about algorithms and test them in code.

An algorithm is a clear, finite set of instructions that transforms input into output. The recipe analogy is useful: the ingredients are inputs, the ordered instructions are the algorithm, and the finished dish is the output. A correct algorithm must terminate and produce the intended result for all valid inputs. In practice, algorithms vary by style — some are iterative, some recursive — but what unites them is determinism and clarity: each step is defined so a computer can execute it. Understanding this definition matters because it separates the idea of correctness from other concerns like implementation details or performance. For example, two algorithms can both solve the same problem correctly, but one may use a loop and the other recursion; both are valid if they terminate and provide the right output for all inputs. A common misconception is to confuse a program or a line of code with an algorithm; think instead of the overall procedure. Finally, notice why explicit steps are important: they let us reason about resources like time and memory, which we analyze next. How would you describe the steps for finding an item on a shelf as an algorithmic recipe?

Efficiency in algorithms refers to two primary resources: time and space. Time is how many computational steps an algorithm requires, typically as a function of input size. Space is how much memory an algorithm needs while it runs. Both matter because a correct algorithm can still be unusable if it demands too much time or memory for realistic inputs. For example, an algorithm that looks fine on a list of ten items might become impractical when that list contains millions. When evaluating efficiency we focus on how requirements grow as input size grows — this reveals scaling behavior. A common beginner mistake is to consider only raw execution time on one machine or on small inputs. That can hide exponential or quadratic growth that quickly becomes impractical. When choosing between algorithms, consider trade-offs: sometimes a faster algorithm needs more memory, and sometimes conserving space costs time. Being able to reason about these trade-offs helps you select the right approach for the problem constraints you face. Ask yourself: what happens to run time and memory when input size doubles? Efficiency: Time and Space means time and space costs determine whether a correct algorithm scales to real inputs; analyze both when choosing solutions.. In practical terms, why we measure resource use and how it affects practical choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Big O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's growth rate as input size 'n' becomes large. It abstracts away constant factors and low-order terms so we focus on how runtime or space scales. O(1) means constant time: the operation's cost does not depend on n, such as reading a single array element by index. O(log n) is logarithmic and often appears when an algorithm repeatedly halves the problem, for example in binary search on sorted data. O(n) is linear: cost grows proportionally with the number of items, like scanning every element in a list. O(n log n) commonly shows up in efficient comparison-based sorting algorithms and combines linear and logarithmic behavior. O(n^2) is quadratic and appears in simple nested loops, where doubling n roughly quadruples the work. A key practical point is that, for large n, the highest-order term dominates: we say n^2 grows much faster than n. A common misconception is treating Big O as precise timing; it is a classification of growth, not a stopwatch. Think about which class an algorithm falls into when deciding whether it will scale to larger datasets.

When analyzing an algorithm, we consider three common cases: best, worst, and average. The best case describes inputs for which the algorithm does the least work. For example, a linear search finds the target at the first position — that is O(1) work. The worst case describes inputs that force the algorithm to do the most work; for linear search that is when the target is last or missing, which yields O(n) comparisons. The average case considers typical inputs assuming a probability distribution; for linear search with a uniformly random target present, you expect about n over 2 comparisons, which Big O simplifies to O(n). We usually report worst-case complexity because it provides a guarantee: no matter the input, the algorithm will not be slower than that bound. A common misconception is assuming average-case measurements guarantee performance in adversarial settings; they do not. Choosing to focus on worst-case is a conservative decision that helps when inputs may be adversarial or unpredictable. Reflect: can you think of an algorithm where average-case is more informative than worst-case? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Linear search is the most straightforward way to find a target in an unsorted list: check each element in sequence until you either find the target or reach the end. Start at the first element, compare it to the target, and if it matches return its index. If not, move to the next element and repeat. This method always terminates for a finite list. Its simplicity is its strength: it requires no preprocessing or sorted order. The trade-off is efficiency: in the worst case it examines every element, giving O(n) time complexity. A useful concrete example is searching for a name in an unsorted contact list; you scan entries one by one. A common misconception is that linear search is always slow; for small lists or when targets are frequently near the front it can be perfectly acceptable. When choosing linear search, ask whether the list is unsorted and whether occasional linear scans are acceptable for your expected input sizes. Fifth, when analyzing algorithms, consider best, worst, and average cases; worst-case gives conservative guarantees, while average-case requires assumed input distributions. Finally, linear search is simple and correct for unsorted lists but has linear worst-case time; when elements are strings include per-comparison string length in your analysis. These points form a checklist you can use when reading or writing code: define the algorithm, identify the dominant operations, account for per-element costs, and classify growth using Big O.

Keep three compact reminders in mind as you work. First, always ask what the dominant operation is — count that to estimate time complexity. Second, include any per-element costs, such as string comparison length, since total cost multiplies these factors. Third, prefer worst-case complexity for guarantees unless you have a clear and justified input model for average-case claims. These short heuristics help you make quick decisions: whether to accept a simple algorithm like linear search or invest in preprocessing or a more sophisticated method. They also make code reviews and design conversations more precise, because you can point to dominant costs and show how they scale with input size.
